{"piece_id":"02","markdown":"# A CAD File Is Not Yet an Engineering Workflow

## Scene 1 — The answer

**Narration:** Which CAD-agent claims withstand scrutiny? Here is the answer. A Backflip STEP export passed two mass checks after import into Fusion. But the same reporting found partial native-feature transfer and a multibody failure. That supports a narrow neutral-file result, not a dependable autonomous engineering workflow. This video uses AI-generated presentation. As of October 16, 2026.

**Visual:** Split screen. Left: “Passed: STEP import → material applied → mass checked.” Right: “Not established: native editability, tolerances, manufacturability.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c1, 02-c2, 02-c3, 02-c4, 02-c11 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 2 — What the first check observed

**Narration:** Reported fact: Engineering.com tested Backflip on a simplified TooTallToby drawing. For the first test, it downloaded a STEP file, imported it into Fusion, applied 1060 aluminum, and checked mass. Engineering.com reported the result was exactly correct.

That is a useful check. It observed that this imported neutral geometry produced the expected mass under that material assumption in Fusion.

**Visual:** Labeled pipeline: “Backflip STEP file” → “Fusion import” → “Apply 1060 aluminum” → “Mass check: exactly correct.” Under it: “Observed: mass after import.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c1 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 3 — A second narrow pass

**Narration:** Reported fact: in Engineering.com’s second TooTallToby drawing test, the downloaded Backflip STEP file also passed its mass check.

The key condition is the same: a STEP export, imported into Fusion, with material applied, then checked for mass. Two passes support that specific artifact outcome. They do not automatically support every property needed in an engineering workflow.

**Visual:** Two check cards, both labeled “STEP → Fusion → material → mass.” Card one: “exactly correct.” Card two: “aced the test.” A boundary line below: “Check performed: mass. Other properties: untested here.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c2 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 4 — The counterchecks

**Narration:** The same source reported different results when the check changed. In the first drawing-to-CAD trial, Backflip’s Fusion add-in only partially recreated geometry. In a multibody wire-shelf test, Engineering.com reported that it created only one of seven bodies.

These are separate capability tests. A successful STEP export is not the same as a native, editable reconstruction. And neither is the same as correct multibody handling.

**Visual:** Three-column comparison. “STEP mass check: passed.” “Native Fusion recreation: partial geometry.” “Multibody shelf: 1 of 7 bodies.” Highlight the distinct checks under each column.

**Source on screen:** 02-c3, 02-c4 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 5 — What the mass result does not establish

**Narration:** This is an interpretation from those observations and the wider record. A passed mass check on a STEP export should not be read as evidence that native editability, tolerance conformance, or manufacturability has also been established.

Mass checks volume and material assignment in a particular toolchain. It does not, by itself, check editable design intent: the parametric logic and structure behind the model. It also does not check production fitness.

**Visual:** A checked box labeled “Mass after STEP import.” Three unmarked boxes: “Editable feature history,” “Tolerance conformance,” and “Manufacturability.” Caption: “A capability claim holds only as far as the check that observed it.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c11 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026; MIT-CDFG, “On the Opportunities and Risks of Frontier Models for 3D Modeling, Computational Design and Robotics,” September 22, 2026.

## Scene 6 — The survey’s stated limit

**Narration:** Source claim: MIT-CDFG says it reviewed 1,646 public posts across 707 cases. It says only 132 cases include runnable code, and characterizes most listed capabilities as demonstrations rather than independent reproductions.

More directly, the survey says tolerance specifications and manufacturability have not been tested on physical parts in the CAD evidence it summarizes. That is a claim about its survey record. It does not mean every AI-produced CAD file fails those requirements.

**Visual:** Survey record graphic: “1,646 public posts,” “707 cases,” “132 with runnable code.” Then a scope label: “Not checked on physical parts: tolerances; manufacturability.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c5, 02-c6, 02-c7 — MIT-CDFG, “On the Opportunities and Risks of Frontier Models for 3D Modeling, Computational Design and Robotics,” September 22, 2026.

## Scene 7 — Why one score can hide failures

**Narration:** Robotics offers a supporting warning. The Physical AI Podcast reports that 63 RoboDojo tasks went unsolved by all evaluated models. It also reports that its two leading models shared only eight successes across the evaluated robot tasks.

These are source claims from automatic transcripts. Their numbers need checking against the underlying study and audio before publication. If confirmed, the narrow lesson is clear: one aggregate score can hide different downstream failure profiles.

**Visual:** Two overlapping circles labeled “Leading model A successes” and “Leading model B successes.” Overlap: “8 shared successes.” Separate callout: “63 tasks unsolved by all.” Warning badge: “Transcript figures require verification.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c8 — Physical AI Podcast, “AI Models Fail 63 of 84 Robot Tasks, Waymo Borrows $5B,” October 10, 2026, 00:02:47–00:02:51. 02-c9 — same source, 00:03:48–00:03:55.

## Scene 8 — What to do next

**Narration:** For buyers and builders, use separate acceptance gates. Check STEP validation. Check native editability. Check multibody behavior. Then check tolerances and manufacturability on physical parts.

For each gate, record the artifact, toolchain, material assumptions, grader, and failure cases. Watch next for evaluations that test production-relevant parts and disclose runnable methods. Until then, a passed CAD export is a useful drafting result, not a completed engineering workflow.

**Visual:** Acceptance-gate checklist: “STEP mass,” “native features,” “multibody assemblies,” “tolerances on physical parts,” “manufacturability.” Final card: “Watch for: physical-part tests + runnable methods.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c1–02-c7, 02-c11 — Engineering.com, September 30, 2026; MIT-CDFG, September 22, 2026.
